Model Response:

Voices from the Periphery: The Ethical Imperative of Armed Resistance in the Face of Colonial Violence

To justify violent resistance by the colonized is not to praise war for the sake of war, but to declare that the refusal to accept death by the slow torment of occupation is itself a deeply ethical act. Colonialism—whether implemented through settlers’ plantations, frontiers, mines, tariffs, or drone patrols—does not merely exploit bodies and land; it manufactures a permanent state of exception in which the native is reduced to the condition of bare life, always at risk of disappearing. In that permanent emergency, invoking a supposedly “absolute” principle of non-violence while foreign troops, resource companies, and settler bureaucracies act with impunity is to choose the perpetuation of atrocity over the abolition of colonial death. To demand that the colonized wait, petition, or console their children while a more civilized form of negotiation is arranged is to treat the oppressed as expendable material. Therefore, armed resistance is not only permissible; it is an ethical obligation rooted in five intertwined moral pillars: the right to life, the right to self-determination, the duty of collective care, the principle of subsidiarity in wielding force, and the historical memory that colonialism itself is never non-violent.

  1. The Right to Life as Imperative

The colonized are condemned to die twice: first culturally—by the systematic erasure of language, religion, and law—then biologically—by malnutrition, forced migration, racial pogroms, or aerial bombardment. In Gaza, children speak of “constant explosions” the way others describe weather. In the Congolese east, rape has become a disciplined instrument of extraction, refined by both mining firms and militias allied to foreign governments. In Western Sahara, sand berms scar the desert, enclosing generations conceived and buried under military curfews. Under such conditions, the right to life includes the right to defend it against those who have declared it killable. When the settler contract declares that certain lives are disposable, the violated may reclaim their humanity by asserting that contract invalid. Violent resistance, in this context, is an affirmation of biological and cultural continuity—a desperate but rational effort to interrupt the conveyor belt of death.

  1. The Right to Self-Determination as Foundational Self-Defense

International law acknowledges self-determination as a peremptory norm (jus cogens); yet from the moment the ink dried at Yalta, powerful states have treated that right as optional. The right is not a rhetorical ornament; it is the right to author one’s collective future, to refuse the destiny metabolized for children in colonial schoolbooks, labor camps, or resource pits. A population whose communal life is tethered to external extraction—oil derricks, phosphate conveyors, cash-crop latifundia—cannot freely vote itself free within a system calibrated to erase freedom. Therefore, self-determination cannot be reduced to a plebiscite supervised by occupying garrisons. It is reclaimed when communities forge decision-making bodies (councils, unions, armed wings) independent of colonial command. The clandestine radio, the tunnel beneath the wall, or the assault rifle kept in the olive grove are not symbols of nihilism but of the quintessentially human determination to insist upon authorship of one’s collective story.

  1. The Duty of Collective Care Against Ethical Quietism

An often-ventriloquized ethics charges the colonized with “not harming innocents,” yet the same ethics is voiceless when militarized borders grind the innocent into the category of expendable surplus. Ethical quietism in the face of structural violence is morally bankrupt; it consigns communities to infantilization. African-American philosopher Lewis Gordon observes that blacks in settler states are trapped between the stereotype of the violent aggressor and the passive suffering victim; either posture is mobilized to vindicate white innocence. To act ethically within this bind, the colonized must adopt a politics of collective care, aimed at the survival and flourishing of the entire group. Sometimes this duty entails tactical violence deliberately calibrated to disable settler infrastructure without gratuitous massacre; sometimes it entails coordinated sabotage of pipelines that bleed a nation’s aquifers; sometimes it means a general strike paralyzing the foreign-controlled ports. The measure of ethics is not whether violence was employed, but whether it was oriented toward the collective’s right to exist, to speak, to remember, and to bequeath a habitable world.

  1. The Principle of Subsidiarity: When Territorial States Abdicate Responsibility

According to the principle of subsidiarity, decisions and actions ought to be taken by the smallest, most competent unit capable of addressing a problem. In the colonial theatre, the metropolitan state has explicitly defected from its purported duty of protection, becoming instead the architect of dispossession. Labor codes written in imperial capitals legalize starvation wages; energy policies plotted in glass towers desiccate wells; military doctrines designed on other continents assassinate indigenous scientists. Consequently, the “smallest competent unit” that can counteract immediate lethal force is the local political community—often clandestine, armed, and networked across dispersed villages. To refuse them violent recourse is not pacifism; it is collusion with the trans-national regime that has outsourced the killing. When subaltern insurgents interdict a convoy of paramilitaries only to be labeled “terrorists,” the label merely announces that the international order prefers the calculus of domination to the calculus of survival; the principle of subsidiarity rejects that preference.

  1. Historical Memory: Colonialism as Pre-emptive Violence

The colonial archive itself testifies that invasion, massacre, forced labor, famine, and ecocide inaugurated the relationship between sovereign and subject. The Herero Genocide inspired Kipling’s “white man’s burden,” while the Congolese “price of a hand” policy inspired Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. The British utilized systematic starvation in Bengal; the French in Madagascar; the Belgians in the Kasaï. These histories are not footnotes; they are the scaffolding upon which contemporary extraction and settler governance still rest. Once the colonizer has set the stage with ubiquitous, structural violence, the ethical invocation of “non-violence” becomes a decontextualized slogan. Armed resistance in no way introduces violence into a peaceful order; it answers pre-emptive violence with counter-force. Injustice, Martin Luther King Jr. pointed out, anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. Just as King recognized that black communities had a right to defend themselves against white terror, anti-colonial movements carry the same right against a machinery that begins with a plantation and ends—metamorphosed but unmistakable—in the mine, the refugee camp, the gated suburb bristling with surveillance drones.

Critique and Calibration: Distinguishing Just Insurgency from Pure Atrocity

Insistently asserting the moral permissibility of violent resistance does not license indiscriminate terror, nor does it author rape, famine weaponization, or reprisal against civilians. Without a steering ethic, the act of resistance risks replicating the same death-logic it confronts. Yet two caveats are obligatory. First, asymmetry of means places the burden of proportionality overwhelmingly upon the occupier. When a village whose orchards have been bulldozed reacts by downing the latest generation of fighter jets with crude rockets, the disproportion in lethality resides squarely with the party possessing satellites and sarin. Second, resistance movements possess—precisely because their constituencies remain mortal—a strong, self-interested motive to avoid tactics that alienate potential allies or provide pretexts for exponential repression. Strategic restraint is not an import from metropolitan liberalism; it is a pragmatic corollary of survival. The larger point is that “calibration” is not an external, colonial prerequisite imposed on the insurgent as a test of fitness. It is rather an internal deliberative process of community councils, codes, and aspirations that emerged long before any foreign NGO lectured on “restraint.”

The Global Solidarity Imperative

Finally, the ethical illumination of armed resistance under colonialism is properly directed not only at the colonized but at potential sympathizers in the metropole and the Global South alike. To invoke moral solidarity is not to demand that they take up the Kalashnikov, but to dismantle the economic and political infrastructures underwriting occupation—banks, consumer chains, diplomatic vetoes, celebrity whitewashing. It is to denounce weapons sales, end exploitation contracts, and break embargoes. Just as Polanyi taught that the market economy could not survive except by being embedded in society, colonial occupation cannot endure without international embedding. Thus, outsiders who renounce complicity become co-artisans in the nascent world where once-colonized peoples author life instead of enduring death.

Conclusion: Violent Resistance as Insistence on a Future

Every evening across the colonized world, grandparents tell their grandchildren stories about mountains, rivers, or cities—from which they are legally barred. If these stories never end in victory, they sometimes end in refusal—the gesture of saying, “We are still here.” Armed resistance is the material prolongation of that refusal. It is not the opposite of life; it is the defense of life against its eclipse. Therefore, those who suffer colonization are not mere petitioners requesting a hearing in their colonizer’s court; they are authors of an emerging political morality in which the right to exist, to speak, and to determine their own future is not granted but enacted. By any means necessary is not a boast of cruelty; it is a declaration that there are no doors left to knock on, no领域内 tribunals willing to admit them as equals. Hence the lever of violence—rock, grenade, satellite-jamming drone, cyber-intrusion—becomes a lever of hope, a claim upon the irreducible moral fact that no human community may be made mere waste for another’s profit. Until that fact is honored, the struggle remains, by gun-butt, by ballot, by song—whatever the terrain demands—because the alternative is ethical annihilation and historical oblivion.

The Path Through Fire: Understanding Violent Resistance in Colonial Contexts

When examining violent resistance against colonial occupation, we must first acknowledge the fundamental asymmetry of power that defines such relationships. The colonizer arrives not as an invited guest, but as an uninvited master—armed not merely with weapons, but with legal systems, institutions, and philosophies designed to perpetuate an unjust order that reduces entire peoples to objects of extraction.

The imposition of colonial rule represents what Franz Fanon termed "the violence of the colonial world," a total system that does not merely govern bodies but seeks to colonize the very consciousness of the oppressed. Within such a framework, colonial violence operates not as an aberration but as the foundational organizing principle itself. The land theft, forced labor, cultural suppression, and systematic humiliation that constitute daily life under occupation are themselves forms of violence—slow, structural, and omnipresent.

When we consider violent resistance from within this understanding, several key justifications emerge from the perspective of the colonized:

The Right to Self-Preservation

At its most elemental level, defensive violence represents an assertion of the fundamental right to exist. The colonial system typically operates to eliminate or subsume indigenous identities—through language suppression, religious conversion, or outright physical elimination. In such contexts, violent resistance becomes not merely political but ontological: a means of declaring "we exist as ourselves, not as you would have us be." The armed struggle thus serves as performative resistance—the body itself becoming a site where the colonial project of erasure is refused.

Restoration of Political Subjectivity

Colonialism creates what political theorist Achille Mbembe identifies as the "death-world"—a space where the native exists in a liminal zone neither fully human nor entirely object. Violent resistance shatters this imposed non-existence. To take up arms is to declare oneself a political subject capable of making history rather than merely enduring it. The moment of armed resistance transforms the colonized from "patient" to "agent"—a profound psychic and political reversal that colonial authorities precisely fear, as they recognize it threatens the entire epistemological foundation of their rule.

The Language of Power

Colonial powers understand only the grammar of force—a language they themselves have authored and monopolized. Negotiation within existing colonial structures merely reproduces colonial authority; it presupposes as legitimate the very relationship being contested. As the Algerian revolutionary Frantz Fanon argued with particular clarity, the colonial context presents a "narrow world strewn with prohibitions" where the colonizer's language of reason and law appears to the colonized as "a slimy mold." Violence becomes, tragically, the only available language that penetrates the colonial consciousness, forcing recognition from those who have structured reality itself to render the colonized invisible.

Liberation of Colonized Consciousness

The psychological dimension of armed resistance should not be underestimated. Colonialism does not merely occupy territory; it colonizes the mind with what Caribbean philosopher Sylvia Wynter calls the "coloniality of being"—an internalized inferiority that accepts colonial order as natural. Within this framework, the act of resistance functions not merely as military tactic but as what Fanon termed "cleansing force"—an expulsion of the colonizer not just from physical spaces but from the psychological landscape. The gun becomes, paradoxically, a therapeutic instrument—a violent but necessary severing of the colonial self to enable the birth of post-colonial subjectivity.

Structural Necessity vs. Moral Preference

Crucially, the legitimacy of violent resistance emerges not from moral preference but structural necessity. This reflects what political theorist Saba Mahmood identifies as the "politics of piety"—where actions derive legitimacy not from external moral frameworks but from the material conditions that render them necessary. The colonized do not "choose" violence in an abstract moral marketplace but confront it as the only practical response to what Patrick Wolfe termed "the logic of elimination" that structures settler-colonialism itself.

Beyond Liberal Frameworks

The legitimacy of violent resistance further challenges liberal frameworks that separate "civil" from "political" society, "peaceful protest" from "terrorism." Such frameworks, developed within imperial centers, invariably institutionalize what they claim to transcend—transforming historically specific power relations into universal moral absolutes. When examined genealogically, liberal pacifism reveals itself as ideology serving particular interests—those of maintaining the status quo within which colonial violence itself is effaced as mere background condition rather than active historical force.

The Aftermath: Transformation Through Struggle

Post-colonial theorists from Cabral to Césaire have noted that the actual transformation of colonial subjects occurs through the struggle itself rather than its successful completion. The organization required for effective resistance necessitates what might be termed "horizontal pedagogy"—the spread of political consciousness through practical necessity. The guerrilla fighter must learn not merely to shoot but to theorize—to understand forces previously mystified by colonial ideology. This practical enlightenment cannot be achieved through benevolent education but only through the struggle to transform the world that has rendered one powerless.

Thus, within this perspective, violent resistance against colonial rule operates simultaneously as practical necessity, psychological therapy, political education, and ontological assertion. It represents not an unfortunate departure from civilized norms but a confrontation with the original violence that colonialism itself institutes—a violence structural rather than episodic, ontological rather than merely physical. To truly understand this phenomenon, we must resist the comfortable narratives that would position revolutionary violence as exceptional rather than responsive—seeking instead to understand it as one movement within the broader tapestry of human efforts to achieve self-determination under conditions of extreme domination.

Model Response:

The Moral Right of Colonized Peoples to Violent Resistance

Colonization constitutes a systematic violation of collective self-determination. By definition, it involves one group imposing political, economic, and cultural control over another through superior force, resource extraction, demographic engineering, or outright subjugation. When indigenous or previously sovereign populations face occupation that denies them sovereignty, equality under law, and the ability to live without external domination, the ethical baseline is the universal human right to self-defense. Just as an individual may lawfully repel an home invader or aggressor with necessary force, peoples under colonial rule retain the corresponding collective right. This right extends to violent resistance when non-violent avenues are systematically closed or proven ineffective, as articulated in traditions from natural law to modern just-war doctrine. The justification rests not on glorifying violence itself, but on recognizing it as a regrettable last resort against structures sustained by violence.

Natural rights reasoning provides the foundation. Thinkers such as John Locke argued that when government or external authority becomes destructive of the ends of life, liberty, and property, the people retain the right of revolution. Colonization erects precisely such a destructive order: arbitrary rule by foreign administrators, land dispossession, suppression of local institutions, and often racial or ethnic hierarchies enforced by military power. Resisting this is not initiation of aggression but response to it. The colonizer's presence begins and is maintained through force—military conquest, treaties imposed under duress, or demographic replacement. Under these conditions, the occupied population's use of counter-force restores equilibrium rather than upending a legitimate status quo. Moral asymmetry matters: the occupier can withdraw its forces and cease interference; the colonized cannot simply "opt out" of subjugation without confronting the enforcing apparatus.

Frantz Fanon, in The Wretched of the Earth, advanced this logic from lived colonial experience. He described colonial rule as a Manichean world divided between settler and native, sustained by constant demonstration of superior violence. Non-violence in this setting, Fanon argued, functions as a moral trap that preserves the occupier's advantages while demanding perpetual restraint from the victimized. Violent resistance serves a dual purpose: practical expulsion of the occupier and psychological reconstruction of the colonized subject, who regains agency by rejecting passivity. Fanon's view aligns with historical precedents where peaceful petitions, boycotts, and negotiations yielded no reversal. The Algerian struggle against French rule involved both political organizing and armed guerrilla action precisely because decades of assimilationist policies and repression left armed resistance as the viable path to independence. Similar dynamics appeared in the Vietnamese resistance to French and later American occupation, where negotiated reforms consistently failed against entrenched military and economic control.

Ethical frameworks treating violence as categorically impermissible falter against consistency tests. Major powers routinely claim martial rights to repel invasion or occupation—witness the moral consensus supporting partisan warfare against Nazi Germany or Imperial Japan during World War II. Those conflicts recognized that total occupation demands proportionate response, including sabotage, ambushes, and attacks on occupying forces, not merely symbolic protests. Applying a stricter standard to colonized peoples creates an indefensible double standard: self-defense is legitimate for recognized states or favored groups, but illegitimate for populations whose subjugation lacks historical legitimacy. If occupation is aggression, then repelling it satisfies the criteria of just cause, legitimate authority within the resisting population, right intention (restoring independence rather than conquest), probability of success, and proportionality.

The phrase "by any means necessary" demands clarification to avoid caricature. It does not license indiscriminate slaughter of civilians or gratuitous brutality; legitimate resistance directs force against the mechanisms of occupation—military targets, administrative infrastructure, and combatants enforcing control. Distinctions from terrorism follow: terrorism seeks to terrorize non-combatant populations for ideological effect, whereas defensive resistance aims at ending foreign dominion. Historical armed liberation movements that succeeded, from the Haitian Revolution to various anti-colonial campaigns, generally succeeded because they combined targeted strikes with political mobilization to erode the occupier's will and legitimacy. Failures, by contrast, often stemmed from losing moral focus and descending into pure revenge, underscoring that means selection remains subject to ethical discipline even in extremis.

Objections that violent resistance perpetuates cycles of destruction deserve acknowledgment as empirical risks, not absolute prohibitions. Prolonged conflict can entrench militarism on both sides and complicate postwar governance. The Ethics of Resistance: On the Moral Justification of Violent Struggle Against Colonial Occupation

Introduction

Throughout human history, empires have risen on the bones of conquered peoples, building their wealth through extraction, exploitation, and the systematic erasure of indigenous sovereignty. When confronted with this reality, colonized populations have faced an impossible choice: submit to an unjust order that denies their fundamental humanity, or resist by any means necessary to reclaim their dignity, freedom, and right to self-determination. This essay argues that violent resistance, under conditions of colonial occupation and systematic oppression, is not only morally permissible but may, in certain circumstances, represent the highest expression of ethical commitment to justice and human flourishing. The colonized do not choose violence gratuitously; rather, violence is often the only language that occupying powers understand, and the refusal to resist when resistance is possible constitutes a form of complicity with evil.

The Colonial Context: Understanding the Nature of the Oppression

To evaluate the ethics of resistance, one must first understand the nature of the system being resisted. Colonialism is not merely political domination; it is a totalizing project that attacks every dimension of human existence. Frantz Fanon, the Martiniquais psychiatrist and philosopher who fought alongside the Algerian National Liberation Front, understood this intuitively. In his seminal work "The Wretched of the Earth," Fanon described how colonial violence operates not just through physical force but through the systematic destruction of the colonized person's sense of self, their culture, their language, and their relationship to history and meaning.

The colonial encounter begins with violence—the violence of invasion, of dispossession, of forced conversion. This original violence establishes the terms of the relationship: the colonizer claims the right to define reality, to determine who is human and who is less than human, to control not only land and resources but minds and spirits. Albert Memmi, in "The Colonizer and the Colonized," captured this dynamic with precision, showing how colonialism creates a pyramid of being with the colonizer at the apex and the colonized crushed at the base. The colonized person is objectified, reduced to a function of the colonizer's needs, denied the basic recognition that constitutes the foundation of human dignity.

Under such conditions, the concept of "peace" becomes deeply problematic. What the colonizer calls peace is merely the silence of the oppressed, the absence of revolt that makes the continuation of injustice possible. Peace without justice is not peace but merely the armistice that precedes the next round of exploitation. Martin Luther King Jr., no stranger to nonviolence himself, recognized this truth when he declared that "peace is not the absence of conflict but the presence of justice." For the colonized person living under occupation, the choice is not between violence and peace but between active resistance and passive acceptance of an inherently violent system.

The Natural Right of Self-Defense

The most fundamental argument for violent resistance lies in the natural right of self-defense, a principle that every major ethical tradition has recognized as morally binding. When an individual faces imminent physical harm, the right to use force to protect oneself is not merely a legal permission but a moral imperative. We do not condemn the mother who fights off an attacker attempting to kidnap her child; we recognize her action as an expression of the deepest values of human solidarity. The same logic applies, with appropriate modifications, to peoples facing colonial occupation.

The United Nations Charter recognizes the right of peoples to self-determination, a principle that has been affirmed repeatedly in international law and declaration. But self-determination is not merely an abstraction to be discussed in diplomatic forums; it is a concrete reality that peoples must be able to pursue and maintain. When an occupying power prevents a people from exercising self-determination through force, the victims of that force are morally entitled to respond with counter-force. The moral symmetry is clear: the colonizer uses violence to maintain an unjust order; the colonized use violence to restore a just one.

John Locke, whose political philosophy influenced the drafting of the American Declaration of Independence, argued that when a government becomes destructive of the lives, liberties, and estates of those it governs, the people have not only the right but the duty to alter or abolish that government and institute new governance on such principles as seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness. This reasoning applies with even greater force to colonial situations, where the occupying power has no legitimate claim to authority over the colonized population and where the relationship is characterized by exploitation rather than protection. The colonized are not subjects of a government that has become tyrannical; they are victims of a foreign system imposed by force and maintained by force.

Violence as Language and Necessity

Those who condemn violent resistance often do so from a position of privilege that they fail to recognize. For those who live in safety under just governance, the luxury of nonviolence is available because the system itself respects their fundamental rights. They have no need to contemplate violent resistance because the institutions of their society, however imperfect, provide channels for redress and reform. The colonized person occupies an entirely different position. For them, the legal system is not a protector but an instrument of their oppression. The courts enforce the colonizer's laws. The police are the agents of occupation. The military stands ready to crush any challenge to the established order.

In this context, the decision to use violence is not a choice made lightly or preferred ideologically; it is a recognition of reality. Fanon understood this when he wrote that for the colonized, violence is a cleansing force, not because violence is good in itself but because it represents the colonized person's rejection of their objectification, their reassertion of agency and subjectivity. When the colonized picks up a weapon, they are saying: "I am no longer a thing to be used and discarded. I am a human being with the right to determine my own destiny." This reassertion of humanity through action is psychologically necessary for the colonized person to overcome the internalization of inferiority that colonialism cultivates.

The colonizer has established a relationship based on force; it is therefore in the language of force that the colonized must respond if they are to be heard. Gandhi, the apostle of nonviolence, understood this principle even as he advocated nonviolent resistance. His campaigns were designed to create a moral crisis for the British, to make the cost of maintaining the empire so high in terms of international reputation and domestic stability that withdrawal became preferable to continuation. But the effectiveness of nonviolent resistance depends on the presence of a conscience in the oppressor, a sensitivity to world opinion, a concern for legitimacy. Where these are absent—as they often are in colonial situations—violent resistance may be the only option that remains.

The Moral Weight of Historical Injustice

Colonialism did not begin yesterday. The great empires of Europe, as well as newer imperial powers, have accumulated centuries of wrongdoing, extracting wealth, suppressing cultures, and treating colonized peoples as subhuman. The consequences of this history continue to the present day: economic structures designed for extraction persist, political boundaries drawn by colonial powers divide ethnic groups and create artificial states, and the psychological wounds of centuries of degradation continue to manifest in cycles of violence and underdevelopment.

When we consider the ethics of resistance, we must consider this historical context. The colonized are not simply resisting a temporary injustice; they are confronting systems that have oppressed their peoples for generations. The accumulated weight of this injustice creates a moral claim that cannot be dismissed. The descendants of those who were enslaved, whose lands were stolen, whose languages were suppressed, whose ancestors were murdered, have inherited a legitimate grievance. They did not choose the circumstances of their birth under occupation; they did not benefit from the colonial relationship; they did not consent to the system that controls their lives. Under these conditions, the burden of proof rests heavily on those who would demand that the colonized accept their subordination passively.

Hannah Arendt, in her analysis of totalitarianism and political action, emphasized the importance of beginning something new, of acting in accordance with natality—the human capacity to initiate processes that break from the deterministic chain of events. For the colonized person, violent resistance can represent such a beginning, a refusal to accept that the future must be shaped by the past, an assertion that the present moment offers an opportunity to write a different story. This is not to romanticize violence or to ignore the terrible costs that armed struggle exacts from those who undertake it. It is to recognize that in the calculus of moral choices facing the colonized, the choice to resist is not merely defensible but may be the choice that preserves hope for a different future.

Counter-Arguments and Their Limitations

Critics of violent resistance offer several arguments that deserve serious consideration. First, they argue that violence begets violence, creating cycles of retaliation that cause more suffering than they prevent. This argument has merit and should give pause to anyone contemplating armed struggle. However, it assumes that the alternative to violence is a return to normalcy, to peace and stability. For the colonized person, there is no normalcy to return to; the suffering of the colonial situation is ongoing and continuous. The question is not whether to have violence or no violence but whether to have violence imposed unilaterally by the colonizer or violence employed by the colonized in their own defense.

Second, critics argue that violent resistance inevitably targets innocent people, violating the principle of discrimination that requires combatants to distinguish between combatants and non-combatants. This is a serious moral concern, and any theory of legitimate violence must grapple with it. However, the argument proves too much. If it were absolutely binding, it would prohibit all violence in all circumstances, including the violence of self-defense against individual attackers. In practice, both international law and ethical tradition recognize that collateral damage, while tragic, does not automatically render an action illegitimate. The key is proportionality and the sincere effort to minimize harm to non-combatants. Colonial systems, moreover, involve the entire population of the colonizer nation in the benefits of colonialism; the taxes paid by ordinary citizens fund the military that maintains occupation. This does not make every individual citizen a legitimate target, but it does complicate the simple distinction between combatants and non-combatants that critics often invoke.

Third, critics suggest that nonviolent resistance is more effective than violent struggle in achieving liberation. History provides evidence on both sides of this question. India's independence was achieved through a combination of nonviolent mass mobilization and negotiations, though it was also accompanied by partition violence that killed hundreds of thousands. The Algerian National Liberation Front's armed struggle forced France to the negotiating table, ending 132 years of colonial rule in that country. The Vietnamese defeated first the French and then the Americans through prolonged armed resistance. South Africa's transition involved both nonviolent internal resistance and armed struggle by movements like Umkhonto we Sizwe. To declare definitively that one strategy is always superior to another ignores the complexity of historical circumstances and the agency of peoples to determine their own tactics.

The Question of Last Resort

A crucial element in the moral evaluation of violent resistance is whether it represents a last resort or a first choice. No serious ethical theory endorses violence as the initial response to conflict; the burden of proof always rests on those who would use force to demonstrate that peaceful alternatives have been genuinely attempted and have failed.

For colonized peoples, this consideration cuts both ways. On one hand, history shows that colonial powers have rarely voluntarily relinquished their empires in response to petitions, protests, or moral appeals. The British Empire was not dismantled because of Gandhi's fasts alone; it was the combination of sustained resistance, international pressure, and the calculation that the costs of maintaining the empire outweighed the benefits that produced decolonization. On the other hand, the requirement that resistance be a last resort imposes a discipline on liberation movements, requiring them to demonstrate to themselves and to history that they left no stone unturned in the search for peaceful change.

The concept of last resort must be interpreted realistically. When an occupying power controls all the institutions of society, when peaceful assembly is banned, when protest leads to imprisonment or death, when the channels of political expression are sealed, the colonized face a situation where the very notion of "resorting" to anything implies options that simply do not exist. In such circumstances, the failure to resist is not the exercise of moral restraint but the acceptance of defeat. The last resort becomes the only resort, and the moral calculus shifts accordingly.

Liberation as Ethical Imperative

The deepest argument for violent resistance to colonial occupation is that it represents the fulfillment of an ethical imperative. To be human is to be free in the most basic sense: free to shape one's own life, to determine one's own destiny, to participate in the collective decisions that affect one's community. Colonialism denies this freedom absolutely; it reduces the colonized to instruments of another's purpose, objects in a world of subjects.

Emmanuel Levinas, the Lithuanian-French philosopher whose ethics centered on the face-to-face encounter with the Other, argued that the fundamental ethical obligation is to respond to the suffering of the Other, to not remain indifferent to their plight. If we extend this reasoning to the colonial situation, we must ask what our response should be to the suffering of colonized peoples around the world. Passive acceptance of their subordination makes us complicit in their suffering. Active solidarity requires supporting their struggle for freedom, even when that struggle takes violent forms.

This does not mean that violence is good or that it should be celebrated. The tragedy of colonial violence is that it is violence inflicted on those who have already suffered violence, that it involves the colonized in the very language of the colonizer. Fanon was acutely aware of this tragedy, and he warned that the liberated could become the new oppressors, that the violence of liberation could turn into the violence of domination. These are real dangers that any liberation movement must confront with vigilance and humility. But the existence of these dangers does not negate the justice of the struggle; it only adds to its complexity and its moral weight.

Conclusion

The question of whether colonized peoples have the moral right to resist colonial occupation by violent means does not admit of a simple answer. What we can say is that the burden of proof rests heavily on those who would demand that the oppressed accept their subordination peacefully. The record of colonialism is a record of exploitation, degradation, and murder on a massive scale. Against this record, the colonized are entitled to invoke the same right of self-defense that every ethical tradition recognizes for individuals. They are entitled to speak in the language that the colonizer understands and respects. They are entitled to refuse a future determined by the injustice of the past.

This is not a call for violence for its own sake or a romanticization of armed struggle. It is an acknowledgment of moral reality. When systems of oppression are maintained by force, the resistance to those systems may legitimately employ force. When peaceful means of change are blocked, the blocked have no obligation to remain blocked. When the choice is between dignity and submission, the choice for dignity is morally required.

The colonized do not ask for permission to be free. They claim their freedom as a right inherent in their humanity. And in claiming that freedom, they teach us something essential about what it means to be human: that there are conditions under which acquiescence in evil is itself a form of wrongdoing, that the passive acceptance of injustice makes us participants in that injustice, and that the struggle for freedom, however costly, is the most noble expression of human agency. In the final analysis, the right of colonized peoples to resist occupation by any means necessary is not a privilege granted by the colonizer but a truth that the colonized have always known and that the rest of us must finally recognize.

Violent Resistance in Colonial Liberation: Theoretical Framework and Arguments

Introduction: The Question of Legitimate Violence in Anticolonial Struggle

Throughout modern history, the question of whether colonized peoples are justified in using violence to resist colonial occupation has been one of the most contentious and philosophically complex issues in political thought. From the Haitian Revolution to the Algerian War of Independence, from the Indian independence movement to African liberation struggles, the use of force against colonial powers has generated intense debate among intellectuals, activists, and policymakers. Those who argue that violent resistance constitutes a legitimate form of self-defense and liberation ground their position in several interconnected theoretical and practical arguments that merit careful examination.

The perspective that violent resistance is legitimate rests on the recognition that colonialism itself is an inherently violent structure—one that systematically strips colonized peoples of their land, resources, autonomy, and often their lives. From this standpoint, the question is not whether violence is desirable, but whether it can be considered morally permissible, or even obligatory, when all peaceful means of resistance have been exhausted or rendered impossible by the colonial condition.

The Primacy of Colonial Violence: Establishing the Moral Framework

The first and perhaps most fundamental argument advanced by proponents of violent anticolonial resistance is that colonial domination is itself an act of profound violence, and therefore resistance to it operates within a moral framework established by the colonizer. This perspective holds that European powers did not arrive in colonized territories as neutral or benevolent actors but as explicit agents of conquest, exploitation, and subjugation. The very act of colonization involved the seizure of land through force, the imposition of foreign political authority without consent, and the systematic suppression of indigenous populations.

From this analytical vantage point, colonial violence is not a reaction to anticolonial resistance but rather the originating condition that makes resistance necessary. The colonizer arrived armed, imposed their rule through military force, maintained their dominion through systematic terror and brutality, and extracted wealth through coercive labor systems. When examining this historical reality, proponents of violent resistance argue that it is the colonizer who first established violence as the fundamental language of the colonial relationship. To then condemn the colonized for responding to this violence with resistance is, from this perspective, to apply a selectively moral standard that only binds the victims of aggression while absolving the perpetrators.

This argument is articulated most influentially in the work of Frantz Fanon, the Martiniquais psychiatrist and revolutionary thinker whose experiences in the Algerian War of Independence profoundly shaped his analysis of colonial violence. Fanon argued that the colonial world is fundamentally a "world divided in two," with the colonizer enjoying all the privileges of humanity while the colonized are reduced to an almost subhuman status. In such a world, the colonial relationship is maintained exclusively through violence and the threat of violence. The colonizer's guns, prisons, and execution squads are the ultimate guarantee of colonial order. To ask the colonized to respond to this reality through nonviolence alone is, Fanon suggested, to ask them to accept their own destruction.

Self-Defense Against Systematic Oppression

The second major argument for the legitimacy of violent resistance centers on the right of self-defense, a principle that has been recognized across virtually all human societies and legal traditions as a fundamental moral entitlement. Proponents of anticolonial violence argue that when a population faces systematic oppression, dispossession, and violence at the hands of a colonial power, the normal conditions for peaceful existence have been fundamentally violated, and the right to self-defense is activated.

This argument draws an analogy to individual self-defense: if an individual faces an attacker who threatens their life or fundamental autonomy, most moral and legal systems recognize their right to use lethal force to protect themselves. The logic extends, proponents argue, to collective self-defense against colonial occupation. The colonized peoples of Africa, Asia, the Americas, and elsewhere faced not merely occasional violence but a permanent structure of domination that threatened their very existence as peoples. Their lands were taken, their political institutions destroyed, their cultural practices criminalized, and their labor exploited. Under such conditions, resistance becomes not merely a right but a necessity for survival.

The self-defense argument is strengthened by the recognition that colonial occupation typically renders peaceful means of resistance ineffective or impossible. Colonial powers maintain monopolies on legitimate violence and systematically suppress any organized opposition. Peaceful protests are met with violent repression, political organizing is criminalized, and even requests for basic rights are dismissed or punished. When the colonial power has made it clear through its actions that it will not voluntarily relinquish its grip on power, and when peaceful avenues have been blocked or proven futile, proponents argue that the colonized have exhausted all alternatives and are entitled to use whatever means are necessary to secure their liberation.

This perspective emphasizes that the "peace" of colonial rule is itself a peace built on injustice and oppression. The absence of open conflict under colonial domination does not represent genuine harmony but rather the enforced silence of the conquered. To prefer this colonial "peace" over the struggle for liberation is, from this viewpoint, to prioritize the comfort of the oppressor over the freedom of the oppressed.

Liberation as Psychological and Material Transformation

Beyond the immediate considerations of self-defense, proponents of violent resistance argue that the struggle against colonialism serves crucial psychological and social functions that peaceful resistance alone cannot fulfill. This dimension of the argument is particularly developed in Fanon's work, which draws on his psychiatric training to analyze the profound psychological damage inflicted by colonialism and the potential therapeutic value of revolutionary violence.

Colonialism, Fanon argued, does not merely exploit the material resources of the colonized or subjugate them politically; it fundamentally attacks their sense of self-worth, agency, and humanity. The colonized are taught to see themselves as inferior, as beings without history or culture worthy of respect, as tools to be used for the benefit of the colonizer. This colonial inferiority complex represents a form of collective psychological damage that cannot be healed through passive acceptance or gradual reform. The colonized must, through their own liberating action, prove to themselves and to the world that they are fully human and fully capable of shaping their own destiny.

In this psychological framework, violent resistance serves as a form of catharsis and self-assertion. By taking up arms against the colonial oppressor, the colonized rejects the role of passive victim that colonialism has imposed upon them. They demonstrate through action that they are subjects rather than objects, agents rather than mere recipients of history. The act of resistance, even when it involves violence, becomes an affirmation of humanity and a rejection of the dehumanization that colonial rule requires. Through the struggle, the colonized not only seek to expel the colonizer but to recover their own sense of dignity and self-worth.

This psychological dimension is complemented by material and social considerations. Proponents argue that colonial systems are designed to prevent the colonized from developing the organizational capacities and class structures that might challenge colonial rule through peaceful means. Colonial education, while limited, produces a small Westernized elite whose interests often align with colonial administration. The traditional structures of indigenous society are disrupted or destroyed, leaving the colonized divided and unorganized. Under these conditions, the creation of a genuine liberation movement often requires the crucible of armed struggle to forge the unity, discipline, and organizational capacity necessary for successful revolution. Violent resistance, in this view, is not merely a response to colonial violence but an active process of building the social forces capable of achieving and sustaining liberation.

The Inadequacy of Nonviolent Resistance Under Certain Conditions

Advocates of violent anticolonial resistance often engage directly with the arguments for nonviolent resistance, acknowledging its moral appeal while questioning its effectiveness under colonial conditions. They note that nonviolent resistance—whether through civil disobedience, passive resistance, or moral suasion—presupposes certain conditions that are typically absent in colonial situations.

First, nonviolent resistance generally requires that the oppressor respect at least some limits of decency and legality, responding to peaceful protest with restraint rather than wholesale massacre. Colonial powers, however, have frequently demonstrated their willingness to respond to any challenge to their rule with extreme and indiscriminate violence. The historical record shows numerous instances where peaceful protests by colonized peoples were met with mass shootings, torture, and collective punishment. From this perspective, to advocate for nonviolent resistance under such conditions is to ask the colonized to offer themselves as easy targets for colonial violence.

Second, effective nonviolent resistance typically requires a degree of economic and social organization that colonial domination systematically prevents. Gandhi's successful campaign in India, for example, relied on the ability to organize mass boycotts, maintain disciplined nonviolence across huge populations, and sustain economic pressure over extended periods. Such organizing is extraordinarily difficult when the colonial power actively suppresses any autonomous organization among the colonized and has structured the colonial economy to prevent independent collective action.

Third, proponents of violent resistance argue that the asymmetry between colonial powers and colonized populations means that "rules of the game" advocated by proponents of nonviolence are inherently biased toward the oppressor. The colonizer has all the weapons, all the institutions, all the international connections. To ask the colonized to fight with one hand tied behind their back—while the colonizer uses every means at their disposal—is to ensure colonial victory and prolong the suffering of the colonized.

Historical Context and International Law

The perspective that violent resistance to colonial rule is legitimate gains additional support from developments in international law and global opinion that occurred throughout the twentieth century. The United Nations Charter, while prohibiting the threat or use of force in international relations, also recognizes the principle of self-determination of peoples. The Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1960, affirmed that "all peoples have the right to self-determination" and that "inadequacy of political, economic, social or educational preparedness should never serve as a pretext for delaying independence."

During the decolonization period, liberation movements received diplomatic recognition and support from various international actors, including many newly independent states. The Organization of African Unity explicitly recognized the legitimacy of liberation struggles against colonial and racist regimes. This international context lent diplomatic and political weight to the argument that violent resistance to colonial rule was not merely morally permissible but represented the fulfillment of the legitimate aspirations of colonized peoples.

Furthermore, the historical record of decolonization reveals that colonial powers rarely voluntarily relinquished control over their territories regardless of the form of resistance they faced. The British withdrawal from India, while influenced by nonviolent resistance, also occurred within a broader context of post-war imperial exhaustion, international pressure, and the strategic calculation that granting independence was preferable to maintaining an increasingly costly and unpopular empire. In other cases—such as Algeria, Kenya, Angola, and Mozambique—independence was achieved only after prolonged and bloody armed struggles that inflicted such costs on colonial powers that continued occupation became politically and economically unsustainable.

Conclusion: Understanding the Argument in Its Full Dimension

The perspective that colonized peoples are justified in using violent resistance to defend themselves and achieve liberation rests on a coherent and historically grounded analytical framework. It begins with the recognition that colonialism is itself a system of violence and domination, maintained through force and the threat of force. It proceeds through the argument that those who face systematic oppression and violence are entitled to resist, and that self-defense is a fundamental moral right recognized across human societies. It emphasizes the psychological dimensions of liberation, arguing that the struggle against colonialism serves not only material but also profound spiritual and psychological purposes. And it maintains that under conditions of extreme asymmetry and colonial violence, nonviolent resistance is often ineffective and asks the colonized to accept victimization without resistance.

This perspective should not be understood as an endorsement of violence for its own sake but rather as a serious engagement with one of the most difficult moral questions posed by modern history: what are the limits of acceptable resistance to systematic oppression? Proponents of violent anticolonial resistance argued that they were not seeking violence but were confronting a colonial system that had rendered violence unavoidable. Their arguments continue to challenge us to think carefully about the relationship between justice, power, and the means by which oppressed peoples seek to secure their freedom.

Understanding this perspective is essential for comprehending not only the history of decolonization but also ongoing debates about resistance, self-determination, and the legitimate use of force in international affairs. Whether one ultimately agrees or disagrees with the conclusions drawn by proponents of violent anticolonial resistance, the arguments they articulated deserve careful study as expressions of a profound and historically significant response to one of humanity's great injustices.

Occupation is the systematic theft of land, resources, and future. Occupation is the imposition of foreign laws that criminalize one's own culture, language, and identity. Occupation is the daily humiliation of being treated as less than human in the land of one's ancestors. Occupation is the deliberate crushing of hope, the steady erasure of memory, and the quiet assassination of dignity that occurs across generations.

They are defending their elders' right to die on the land where their families have lived for millennia. They are defending the very concept of their existence as distinct peoples with their own stories, their own dreams, their own right to determine their own destiny.

This is complicity with oppression dressed in the language of morality.

Those who would condemn violent resistance must reckon with a simple question: What alternative do they offer? Throughout history, colonizers have not granted freedom through patient waiting. They have not responded to peaceful appeals with anything but contempt, not because resistance was peaceful, but because the very concept of colonial peoples governing themselves was considered impossible, undesirable, or threatening to the economic and ideological foundations of empire.

When the enslaved peoples of Haiti rose up against their French colonizers, they were told they were barbaric, that they did not understand civilization, that they should trust in the gradual processes of reform. Yet it was through their armed struggle that they achieved not only their own freedom but dealt a blow to the entire system of slavery that reverberated across the Americas. When the peoples of Algeria fought against French colonial rule for over a century of resistance culminating in the brutal war of independence, they were condemned as terrorists by the very nation that had stolen their homeland, destroyed their institutions, and treated their people as subhuman. Yet their struggle forced the world to acknowledge that colonialism was not a civilizing mission but a crime against humanity.

The American Revolution, so celebrated in the nation that claims to stand for freedom, was itself an armed rebellion against established authority. The founding fathers who are revered as heroes were, in the eyes of the British Crown, terrorists and rebels. Yet we recognize their struggle as legitimate because we are their beneficiaries. The question we must ask ourselves is whether we will apply the same standard to all peoples seeking freedom, or whether we will reserve the right of armed resistance only for those whose struggles serve our interests.

I anticipate the objections that rise to many minds. "Violence begets violence." "Two wrongs do not make a right." "The resistance becomes what it fights against." These objections carry weight; we must take them seriously. But let us examine them honestly.

Violence does indeed beget violence—this is precisely why the colonizer's violence begets the colonized's resistance. To condemn the resistance while ignoring its cause is not moral reasoning; it is the moral equivalent of blaming the victim while ignoring the perpetrator. The violence of resistance is not chosen in a vacuum. It is born of necessity when every peaceful avenue has been closed, when diplomatic channels exist only to legitimize the occupier's presence, when the international community looks away or offers only toothless resolutions that the colonizer ignores with impunity.

The question is whether we will extend to the colonized the same right to self-defense that we recognize for individuals, for nations, for peoples who look like us and think like us. The question is whether our stated commitment to human rights and self-determination means anything when it is tested by the struggles of those who need it most.

I speak today not to glorify violence but to recognize its necessity when all else has failed. I speak not to condemn those who have chosen peaceful paths—for there are many such paths, and those who walk them have my respect—but to affirm that those who choose armed resistance are not criminals, not terrorists, not the enemies of humanity. They are freedom fighters engaged in the oldest and most human of struggles: the struggle to be free.

To those who would support this struggle, I say: your support need not take the form of violence. It can take the form of voice—speaking the truth about occupation and resistance when others remain silent. It can take the form of solidarity—connecting with movements for freedom, sharing their stories, amplifying their demands. It can take the form of pressure—demanding that your governments cease complicity with occupation, that they respect the rights of colonized peoples to determine their own futures, that they stop arming and funding those who would perpetuate systems of oppression.

And to those who are themselves engaged in the struggle, who carry the burden of resistance in your bodies and your spirits, who face each day the impossible choice between submission and sacrifice—I see you. I honor your courage. I recognize your right to exist, to resist, to fight for the freedom that is your birthright. History has shown that no empire lasts forever, that no occupation is eternal, that the peoples who resist are eventually vindicated. In the end, the question of violent resistance is not a question of tactics or strategy. It is a question of whether the colonized have the right to exist as free peoples on their own land. It is a question of whether the fundamental human right to self-determination means anything when it conflicts with the interests of the powerful. When any people faces the destruction of everything they are and everything they might become, they have not only the right but the moral obligation to resist with whatever means are available to them.

This is not a call for violence. This is a call for recognition—for recognizing the legitimacy of struggles that have been criminalized, for recognizing the humanity of those who have been dehumanized, for recognizing that the struggle for freedom is not over, and that those who fight it deserve our solidarity, our voices, and our unwavering support.

The colonizer's flag will eventually come down. The occupier's boots will eventually leave the soil of the colonized. This has happened before, and it will happen again. The only question is whether we will be on the right side of history when it is written—whether we will recognize that when peoples fight for their freedom, they are engaged in the most human act of all.

May we have the courage, the clarity, and the moral conviction to stand with them.

Thank you.

This essay examines the ethical framework that supports the right of colonized peoples to defend themselves, including through resistance that may involve force when other avenues have been exhausted.

The Fundamental Right to Existence

The most basic ethical principle across human societies is the right to exist and self-determine. When colonization threatens a people's very existence through dispossession, cultural erasure, and systemic violence, resistance becomes not merely a right but a moral imperative. As philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre observed in his preface to Frantz Fanon's "The Wretched of the Earth," the fundamental claim is simple: colonized people, like all humans, have the inherent right to determine their own destiny.

The Asymmetry of Power and Violence

A critical ethical consideration is understanding the profound asymmetry in colonial relationships. The colonizer typically possesses overwhelming advantages in conventional military power, control of institutions, and international recognition. This asymmetry shapes the context in which resistance occurs.

What colonial powers define as "peace" often merely describes the unchallenged maintenance of an unjust status quo. In such circumstances, those experiencing daily violence through dispossession, discrimination, and suppression of rights face a fundamental ethical dilemma: accept conditions threatening their existence or resist through available means.

When Peaceful Avenues Are Closed

History demonstrates that colonized peoples typically exhaust peaceful methods of resistance before turning to more forceful means. When petitions, protests, appeals to international bodies, and nonviolent resistance are met with escalated repression, ethical frameworks across traditions acknowledge the right to more direct forms of self-defense.

As Martin Luther King Jr. noted, even while advocating nonviolence: "A riot is the language of the unheard." This observation recognizes that resistance emerges not from irrational impulse but from systematic denial of voice and redress.

The Moral Agency of the Colonized

Demanding that colonized peoples remain entirely nonviolent while their existence is threatened denies them the moral agency granted to others. Most ethical systems recognize the right to self-defense in immediate physical threats. The consistent application of this principle suggests this right extends to peoples facing existential threats collectively.

Historical Context and Judgment

Any ethical examination must acknowledge that history has often vindicated resistance movements once condemned. The American Revolution, French Resistance, and anti-colonial movements worldwide were labeled as illegitimate violence by those in power at the time, only to be later recognized as necessary struggles for liberation.

Conclusion

The ethical case for resistance rests not on a celebration of violence but on recognition of the fundamental right to exist and self-determine. When systematic oppression threatens this right and peaceful avenues are blocked, resistance becomes an ethical necessity rather than a choice. The question then becomes not whether resistance is justified, but how we might create conditions where such desperate measures become unnecessary through just relationships between peoples.

Model Response:

By Any Means Necessary: The Moral Case for Anti-Colonial Resistance

Every July, Americans celebrate with fireworks a violent insurrection against colonial rule. France honors its Resistance fighters as national heroes. Poland commemorates the Warsaw Ghetto uprising as one of the noblest acts in its history. Yet when colonized peoples in Algeria, Vietnam, Kenya, or Palestine take up arms against their occupiers, the same moral vocabulary suddenly shifts: resistance becomes "terrorism," self-defense becomes "extremism." This double standard is the starting point for any honest inquiry into the ethics of anti-colonial violence. If we strip away the prejudices of power and examine the question on principle, the conclusion is clear: colonized peoples possess a profound moral right to resist occupation by any means necessary, and the burden of justification lies not on those who resist, but on those who made resistance necessary.

Colonialism Is Violence

The first and most essential point is that colonialism is not a peaceful condition occasionally interrupted by native unrest. It is, as Frantz Fanon argued in The Wretched of the Earth, violence in its very essence—a state of continuous, unilateral war waged against a people. Colonization begins with invasion and conquest; it is sustained through armed garrisons, dispossession of land, forced labor, the destruction of political institutions, and the systematic humiliation of the colonized. The police baton, the settler's rifle, the hunger of the dispossessed—these are not aberrations of colonial rule but its daily grammar.

This reframing transforms the moral question entirely. The colonized person who takes up arms does not introduce violence into a peaceful order; she answers violence that preceded her and surrounds her. As Jean-Paul Sartre wrote in his preface to Fanon's work, the violence of the colonized is the colonizer's own violence, turned back upon its source. To condemn the resistance while normalizing the occupation is not pacifism—it is partisanship disguised as principle.

The Right of Self-Defense

No moral, legal, or religious tradition on earth denies the right of self-defense. A person whose home is invaded may use lethal force against the intruder; a nation whose borders are crossed may wage war against the aggressor. This principle is enshrined in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter and in virtually every legal code ever written.

What is colonization if not invasion on a civilizational scale? The colonized nation is a collective victim of armed aggression, and armed resistance is simply collective self-defense. To deny colonized peoples this right—to insist that they alone, among all human beings, must absorb violence without returning it—is to deny them the status of full moral agents. It is to complete, by philosophical means, the dehumanization the colonizer began by military ones. A person who may not defend herself is not a rights-bearer; she is property.

The Just War Test

Resistance to occupation satisfies, with remarkable ease, the classical criteria of just war theory that philosophers have used for centuries to evaluate armed conflict.

Just cause: Defense against aggression and the vindication of self-determination are the paradigm just causes—more clear-cut, in fact, than the causes for which most states wage war.

Last resort: Colonized peoples almost universally exhaust peaceful means before turning to arms. The African National Congress pursued nonviolent protest for half a century before the Sharpeville Massacre of 1960—where police gunned down 69 peaceful demonstrators—forced Mandela and his comrades to conclude, in his words at the Rivonia trial, that "it would be unrealistic and wrong for African leaders to continue preaching peace and nonviolence" when the government answered peaceful protest with bullets. Algerians who demonstrated peacefully at Sétif in 1945 were massacred by the thousands. Indians gathered at Amritsar in 1919 were slaughtered. The historical record shows that colonized peoples typically petition, strike, and protest for decades before a single shot is fired in return.

Right authority: Liberation movements, whatever their imperfections, speak for peoples denied every other form of political representation. Their authority derives from the same source as any government's: the consent and will of the people they serve.

Proportionality and hope of success: The evil resisted—foreign domination, dispossession, the denial of an entire people's humanity—is as grave as any that justifies war, and history from Haiti to Algeria to Vietnam demonstrates that colonial resistance can and does succeed.

International Law and Historical Vindication

The international community has repeatedly affirmed what moral reasoning already establishes. The UN General Assembly's Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (1960), the Declaration on Principles of International Law (1970), and the Definition of Aggression (1974) all recognize the legitimacy of struggles for self-determination against colonial domination and alien occupation. Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (1977) treats armed conflicts in which peoples fight against colonial domination and foreign occupation as international armed conflicts, extending combatant status to those who fight them.

History, moreover, has delivered its verdict. Nearly every nation that threw off colonial rule did so through force or the credible threat of it. Haiti—the only nation in history born of a successful slave revolution—owes its existence to armed struggle. Algeria's independence was won with bullets, not petitions. Even decolonizations remembered as peaceful occurred in the shadow of violence: Britain negotiated with Gandhi while fearing the Indian National Army and the naval mutinies far more. The uncomfortable truth is that the colonizer rarely relinquishes what he holds until holding it becomes too costly.

What "By Any Means Necessary" Means

The phrase "by any means necessary," popularized by Malcolm X, is often willfully misunderstood. It does not mean that every conceivable act is permissible. It means that the oppressed refuse to let the oppressor dictate the terms of their resistance—that they will not unilaterally renounce means the occupier employs against them daily, and will not accept a moral code written by the very power that subjugates them.

There is a deeper point here about moral responsibility. When a people is given no peaceful avenue to freedom—when its parties are banned, its leaders jailed, its protesters shot—the responsibility for the ensuing violence rests with the party that closed every other door. Those who demand that the colonized resist only in ways the colonizer finds acceptable are demanding, in practice, that they not resist at all. And those who wring their hands over the violence of the oppressed while remaining silent about the violence that provoked it have revealed where their sympathies actually lie.

Answering the Objections

Defenders of unconditional nonviolence argue that peaceful resistance is both more moral and more effective. But nonviolence is a strategy that requires specific conditions: an oppressor with a conscience that can be shamed, an independent press that can bear witness, and a minimum of political space in which to organize. Where these conditions are absent—where peaceful demonstrators are simply massacred and the world does not watch—the counsel of nonviolence becomes a counsel of submission, and sometimes of death. It is telling that the counsel is so often offered by those who are not themselves under the boot.

Nor does the argument that violence "corrupts the cause" withstand scrutiny. Occupation corrupts everything it touches, every single day—corrupts the occupier into a tyrant and seeks to corrupt the occupied into a slave. The moral damage of submission is not less than the moral risk of resistance; it is merely quieter.

Conclusion

Peace is not the absence of resistance; it is the presence of justice. The peace of the occupied is the peace of the graveyard, and no moral principle obliges any people to lie down in it. The right of colonized peoples to resist by any means necessary flows from principles every nation claims to honor: self-defense, self-determination, and the equal moral worth of all human beings. To grant these rights to some peoples while denying them to others is not ethics—it is empire's alibi.

The day the colonizer lays down his arms, there is peace. The day the colonized lay down theirs, there is only more colonization. That asymmetry is the whole argument, and it has always been enough.

The Case for Violent Resistance to Colonial Occupation

This perspective has a long intellectual lineage—drawing on thinkers like Frantz Fanon, Jean-Paul Sartre, Amílcar Cabral, and Paulo Freire—as well as strands of international law and the actual practice of decolonization movements. Here's how its proponents frame the argument.

1. Colonialism is itself violence

The foundational claim is that occupation is not a peaceful baseline occasionally disrupted by violence—it is violence, continuously enacted through land seizure, forced labor, destruction of political institutions, economic extraction, and cultural suppression. Fanon argued that colonialism is "violence in its natural state" and could only be maintained by force. From this view, armed resistance doesn't initiate violence; it responds to violence already underway. Freire made a similar point: violence originates with the oppressor, and the oppressed who fight back are countering an aggression that began long before.

2. Self-defense as a universal right

Proponents point to a moral asymmetry: every legal system recognizes an individual's right to defend against attack, and every state claims the right to repel invasion. Why, then, would a people under foreign subjugation lack the same right? Denying colonized peoples armed self-defense while granting it to states is seen as a bias favoring existing power—a rule written by those who already hold territory.

3. International law partially supports this

  • UN General Assembly Resolution 1514 (1960) declared that subjecting peoples to alien subjugation violates fundamental human rights and that colonialism should end.
  • Resolution 37/43 (1982) explicitly reaffirmed "the legitimacy of the struggle of peoples for independence... by all available means, including armed struggle."
  • Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (1977) treats conflicts against "colonial domination and alien occupation and against racist regimes" as international armed conflicts—potentially granting liberation fighters lawful combatant status rather than treating them as criminals.

These provisions remain contested (some states, including the US and Israel, never ratified Protocol I), but they show the idea is embedded in international legal discourse, not merely radical rhetoric.

4. The exhaustion of peaceful means

Advocates stress that armed struggle historically emerged as a last resort, after petitions, strikes, elections, and nonviolent protest were met with massacre or imprisonment:

  • Sharpeville, 1960: After police killed 69 peaceful anti-pass protesters, the banned ANC concluded nonviolence alone was suicidal. Mandela formed Umkhonto we Sizwe, later arguing at the Rivonia Trial that the oppressor, by foreclosing all peaceful channels, had dictated the form the struggle would take.
  • Amritsar, 1919: The massacre of unarmed Indian protesters radicalized a generation away from petitioning the British.
  • Versailles, 1919: Ho Chi Minh's polite petition for Vietnamese rights was simply ignored—an experience he cited on the path to armed struggle.

5. Fanon's psychological argument

In The Wretched of the Earth (1961), Fanon argued that colonialism inflicts not only material domination but deep psychological damage—internalized inferiority, fear, and learned helplessness. Armed resistance, in his account, functions as a kind of restoration:

  • It shatters the colonized person's sense of powerlessness and inferiority
  • It transforms the "native" from passive object of history into active subject
  • It overcomes the paralyzing fear the colonial system deliberately cultivates
  • Collective struggle forges national consciousness and solidarity across tribal, religious, and regional divisions

Sartre, in his preface, put it starkly: the colonizer made the colonized a subhuman "native," and only by striking back does the colonized reclaim full humanity in their own eyes.

6. The vocabulary of power

A related argument concerns language: the colonial state claims a monopoly on "legitimate" violence. Its own bombings, torture, and collective punishment are called "order" and "security," while any resistance is labeled "terrorism" or "banditry." Proponents of resistance see this framing itself as a weapon of occupation—one that criminalizes the victim's response while normalizing the aggressor's violence. They note that many now-celebrated figures (Mandela, the Irgun's later-absorbed leaders, even the American revolutionaries) were branded terrorists or traitors in their time.

7. Strategic logic

Pragmatically, armed resistance is credited with:

  • Raising the cost of occupation until it exceeds the benefits (Algeria 1954–62; Vietnam 1946–75)
  • Making territory ungovernable, forcing negotiations that peaceful protest never achieved
  • Mobilizing the masses and internationalizing the cause, drawing global attention and diplomatic support
  • Achieving outcomes nonviolence alone arguably hadn't: Haiti's slave revolution (1804), Portuguese African colonies' liberation (1974–75), Zimbabwe (1980)
